gaps.note: Wrong. In the product (D_{a_k}D_{a_{k-1}}^{-1})...(D_{a_1}D_{a_0}^{-1}) everything cancels except D_{a_k} on the left and D_{a_0}^{-1} on the right, so the result is D_{a_k}D_{a_0}^{-1}, not D_{a_k}D_{a_1}^{-1}. The page's own next paragraph uses the source frame D_source(w)^{-1} (the first node), and the paper (lines 143-145) has sink and source endpoints.

gaps.quote: By the telescoping, the route applies
gaps.note: The reader is not told why the route operator has the source frame inverse applied: the page never says that the supplied physical input f is read as the logical array D_in^{-1} f (paper lines 141-142, 797-798), so the stored array at the source is f and not D_source(w) f. Without this the telescoped product is not the operator applied to the supplied input.

gaps.quote: carries a linear operator $D_\nu$ on arrays indexed by the common address set
gaps.note: The page uses D_alpha^{-1} and D_source^{-1} but never states that frames are invertible (paper line 133 and 793: invertible linear operator), nor that all incidences of one gate use the same frame; the commuting identity and the edge operator need both.

gaps.quote: if a route has source frame $I$ and sink frame $D_\nu$, its operator is $D_\nu$
gaps.note: Inconsistent with the page's own formula: a route applies epsilon_w D_sink D_source^{-1}, so with source frame I and sink frame D_nu the route operator is epsilon_w D_nu. It equals D_nu only after the sign is undone, i.e. the endpoint operator (paper lines 819-822).
